title: Elizabeth Fry in Newgate Prison
text:
In 1813 Elizabeth Fry, a Quaker mother of a large family in London, was taken to see the women's section of Newgate Prison. She found some three hundred women and their children crowded into a few rooms, sleeping on the floor in filthy straw, cooking, washing and eating in the same space. Some had been convicted, others were waiting for trial. Visitors were warned that the women were wild and dangerous.

Fry brought clothes, and returned in earnest in 1816. She asked the women what they wanted for their children and, with their agreement, started a school inside the prison, choosing one of the prisoners as teacher. In 1817 she and other Quaker women founded an association to help the women prisoners. They brought in work, sewing and knitting that could be sold, read the Bible aloud, and drew up rules that the prisoners themselves agreed to, with monitors chosen from among them.

Officials were astonished at the change in behavior. In 1818 Fry described her work to a committee of the House of Commons, a rare role for a woman at the time. Her methods spread to prisons across Britain and Europe.
lesson: Treat people as capable of change and give them a say in their own improvement. Respect and responsibility often achieve more than control and contempt.
source: Memoir of the Life of Elizabeth Fry, edited by her daughters (1847); Report from the Select Committee on the Prisons within the City of London (1818)
place: Old Bailey (site of Newgate Prison), London
